statement: In people who use cannabis, using it more often and starting younger are associated with a higher share meeting criteria for dependence in the figures that narrative reviews cite, but most of these figures are second-hand and rest on different designs and definitions, and in the one national survey analysis read that adjusted for other disorders, starting early went with a lower, not a higher, hazard of dependence. By frequency of use (second-hand): 17.0% of people who smoked cannabis weekly and 19.0% of those who smoked daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021, which also calls this almost 1 in 19, although 9.7% is about 1 in 10); 30 to 40% of people with a history of daily use (two reviews cited by Connor et al., 2021) or up to one-third of people who use daily (a UN report cited by the same review); half of people who use daily, from a 3-year prospective study of frequent use (van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015); and 25 to 50% of people who smoke daily, cited to a review that does not contain the figure (Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, 2009), so it cannot be traced. No definitions or adjustment are given with these figures. By age of first use (second-hand): one in six of people who start in adolescence, against about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009, and Hall, 2015, citing a 2006 book chapter; Volkow et al., 2014, citing Hall & Degenhardt, with 17% in its table); people who start in adolescence about 2 to 4 times as likely as people who start as adults to have dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (Chen et al., 2009, as cited by Volkow et al., 2014); and first use before 16 linked to a higher risk and faster progression (Connor et al., 2021, citing three sources). In the 1990-92 US National Comorbidity Survey, by age at interview rather than age at first use, 15.3% (SE 2.3) of people aged 15 to 24 who had ever used cannabis had ever been dependent (DSM-III-R), against 8.1% at 25 to 34, 8.5% at 35 to 44 and 3.1% at 45 to 54, although the youngest had had the fewest years in which to become dependent; the authors cite studies in which people who start illicit drugs before 17 seem at higher risk of drug problems even after allowing for how long they had used (Anthony et al., 1994). In the 2001-05 US NESARC (7,389 adults who had used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence; recalled ages), first use before 14, compared with first use at 14 or later, went with a higher hazard of dependence before adjustment (hazard ratio 2.47) and a lower one after stepwise adjustment for sociodemographic factors, psychiatric disorders and dependence on other substances (0.63, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9), while mood disorders (2.69) and cocaine dependence (4.14) went with higher hazards; the authors read early onset as a marker of other psychiatric and substance use problems rather than a risk factor in itself (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). In a 3-year prospective study of people who used frequently, measures of cannabis use itself did not predict who became dependent, while living alone, using cannabis to cope and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, as described by Curran et al., 2016), and twin studies find shared genetic and environmental influences on starting early (Connor et al., 2021). None of the sources measured how much THC people took, and, in the editors' reading, frequent use is partly built into what dependence means (its criteria include using more, or for longer, than intended and spending a great deal of time using), so the two are hard to separate. Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Reviews report that people who use cannabis more often are more likely to be dependent: figures for people who use daily run from about 1 in 5 to 1 in 2, depending on the study, and one often-quoted figure (25 to 50 in 100) cannot be traced to any study. Reviews also say about 1 in 6 people who start as teenagers become dependent, against about 1 in 10 of everyone who has used. But in a large US survey, starting before age 14 went with more dependence only until other mental health and drug problems were taken into account; after that, it went with less. So it is not clear whether starting young itself raises the risk or whether people who start young are at higher risk for other reasons. Most of these numbers are second-hand, and none of these studies can show cause. See the contested question.
population: People who use cannabis: US national survey samples (1990-92, ages 15 to 54; 2001-05, adults who had used) and the cohorts and surveys cited by narrative reviews for frequency and age of onset (definitions often not given)
exposure: Frequency of use (weekly, daily, a history of daily use, frequent use, as each source defined it) and age at first use (adolescence, before 16, before 14); in one survey, age at interview
comparator: People who use less often or started later; in the 1990-92 survey, older age groups at interview
outcome: Cannabis dependence (DSM-III-R, DSM-IV, or as the cited studies defined it; dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use in one study)
magnitude: Second-hand frequency figures: 17.0% weekly and 19.0% daily meeting dependence criteria; 9.7% of weekly smokers without dependence dependent within a year (Cougle 2016 via Connor 2021); 30-40% with a history of daily use (two reviews via Connor 2021); up to one-third of people using daily (UN report via Connor 2021); half of people using daily (van der Pol 2013 via Hall 2015); 25-50% of daily smokers (Volkow 2014, not traceable). Second-hand age figures: one in six with adolescent onset (book chapter via Hall 2009 and Hall 2015; 17% in Volkow 2014 Table 1); 2-4 times dependence symptoms within 2 years, adolescent against adult onset (Chen 2009 via Volkow 2014). NCS 1990-92 by age at interview, DSM-III-R dependence among people who had used: 15-24, 15.3% (SE 2.3); 25-34, 8.1% (0.7); 35-44, 8.5% (1.3); 45-54, 3.1% (1.5). NESARC 2001-05, first use before 14: unadjusted HR 2.47; adjusted 0.63 (95% CI 0.5 to 0.9); in the adjusted model mood disorder 2.69, personality disorder 2.30, anxiety disorder 2.31, cocaine dependence 4.14 (2.3 to 7.6), alcohol dependence 2.55.

risk_of_bias.note: Surveys and cohorts with self-reported, often recalled, use and ages; the age figures are unadjusted except in NESARC, where adjustment reversed the direction; most frequency figures come with no adjustment set or definition (cards sc_anthony_1994, sc_lopez_quintero_2011, sc_connor_2021).

inconsistency.note: Figures for daily use run from 19% to about half across sources, and the early-onset association points in opposite directions before and after adjustment.

indirectness.note: Most figures are second-hand (narrative reviews; the studies behind them not read here, one a book chapter and one figure untraceable); the 1990-92 age groups are ages at interview, not at first use; DSM-III-R and DSM-IV dependence, not DSM-5 use disorder; frequency categories undefined.

imprecision.note: Not downgraded separately: most figures carry no interval, which is part of the second-hand problem; the one adjusted estimate (0.63, 0.5 to 0.9) excludes 1.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; down one level each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness: very low. Not upgraded for a dose-response gradient: the frequency gradient is second-hand, mostly cross-sectional and partly built into the outcome. Rated as worded, an association; whether frequent or early use causes dependence is the question in the debate box. Overlap: the one-in-six figure reaches three reviews from one source (a 2006 book chapter by the first author of the 1990-92 survey), Hall (2015) repeats Hall & Degenhardt (2009), and one 3-year study (van der Pol et al., 2013) is cited by two reviews for different findings (half of people using daily became dependent, Hall 2015; measures of use did not predict transition, Curran et al. 2016), so these are not independent replications. Status contested: for age of first use, crude figures and an adjusted national analysis point in opposite directions.

debate.question: Does using cannabis more often, or starting it younger, make dependence more likely, or do the people who use often or start young differ in other ways that explain the link?
debate.evidence_yes: Every source that reports dependence by frequency finds more in people who use more often: 17.0% of people who smoked weekly and 19.0% of those who smoked daily met dependence criteria, and 9.7% of people smoking weekly without dependence became dependent within a year (Cougle et al., 2016, as cited by Connor et al., 2021); reviews give 30 to 40% of people with a history of daily use (two reviews cited by Connor et al., 2021) and half of people using daily in a 3-year prospective study (van der Pol et al., 2013, as cited by Hall, 2015), against about 9 in 100 of everyone who has used (see the claim on how many people become dependent). For age of starting, reviews give one in six of people who start in adolescence (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; Volkow et al., 2014), describe people who start in adolescence as 2 to 4 times as likely as adult starters to show dependence symptoms within 2 years of first use (Chen et al., 2009, as cited by Volkow et al., 2014), and cite first use before 16 as raising the risk and speeding progression (Connor et al., 2021). In the 1990-92 US survey, 15.3% (SE 2.3) of 15- to 24-year-olds who had used cannabis had ever been dependent, against 8.1% to 8.5% at 25 to 44 and 3.1% at 45 to 54, although the youngest had had the fewest years at risk, and its authors cite studies in which people who start illicit drugs before 17 seem at higher risk of drug problems even after allowing for how long they had used (Anthony et al., 1994). Reviews also name concurrent tobacco use and male sex as risk factors (Curran et al., 2016).
debate.evidence_no: In the one national analysis read that modelled age of first use together with other risk factors (NESARC, 2001-05; 7,389 adults who had used cannabis; DSM-IV dependence), first use before 14 went with a higher hazard of dependence before adjustment (2.47) but a lower one after stepwise adjustment for sociodemographic factors, psychiatric disorders and dependence on other substances (0.63, 95% CI 0.5 to 0.9), while mood disorders (2.69) and cocaine dependence (4.14) went with higher hazards; the authors read early onset as a marker of other disorders rather than a cause (Lopez-Quintero et al., 2011). A 3-year prospective study of people who used frequently found that measures of cannabis use itself did not predict who became dependent, while living alone, using cannabis to cope and negative life events did (van der Pol et al., 2013, as described by Curran et al., 2016). Twin studies show genetic influence on starting early after allowing for other substance use, conduct disorder, depression and anxiety, and shared genetic or environmental factors contribute to early onset (Connor et al., 2021); a review names poor school achievement, deviant behaviour, rebelliousness, poor relationships with parents and parents' drug and alcohol problems as marking higher risk (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009). The widely quoted 25 to 50% of people who smoke daily is cited to a review that does not contain it (Volkow et al., 2014), and the age-group figures from the 1990-92 survey are by age at interview, not age at first use.
debate.neither_can_show: Whether frequent or early use causes dependence: in every source people chose how often to use and when to start, most figures reach us through narrative reviews, and the sources behind one in six (a book chapter) and 25 to 50% (untraceable) cannot be checked here. Frequency and dependence are entangled: the dependence criteria include using more, or for longer, than intended and spending a great deal of time using (Curran et al., 2016, Box 3), so people may use more often because they are dependent. Ages of first use and of onset were recalled, sometimes decades later. Adjusting for other psychiatric and substance use disorders removes confounding where those disorders came first, but where they followed cannabis use it may also remove part of a real effect (editors' point; the NESARC models entered mood, anxiety and other substance use disorders as time-varying). None of the sources measured how much THC people took (Connor et al., 2021).
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). More frequent use goes with more dependence in every source that reports it, but the size depends on design and definition (from about 1 in 5 to about 1 in 2 of people using daily), most figures are second-hand, and one widely quoted figure cannot be traced. For age of starting, the crude figures point to more dependence in early starters, but the one national analysis that adjusted for other disorders found the opposite, which fits early starting being a marker of other risks at least as well as a cause; the evidence read here does not settle which.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Prospective cohorts that follow people from before first use, with repeated DSM-5 assessments and measured THC exposure (standard units and product strength), reporting the cumulative probability of use disorder by frequency, age of first use and product, with psychiatric problems dated before and after first use; and sibling or co-twin comparisons of early and late starters.

statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether, or how much, cannabis use causes psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia. The association with later psychosis is consistent and stronger with frequent use (see the answer on how often people use), but in the studies read a substantial part of it is explained by measured confounders, and genetically informed studies suggest that a further part reflects shared family or genetic liability, or genetic liability to schizophrenia making cannabis use more likely; none of these designs excludes a causal contribution, and none measures the effect of frequent or high-potency use. Adjustment for each cohort's measured confounders removed on average about 45% (10% to 80%) of the crude excess odds in seven cohorts (Moore et al., 2007). In the one co-relative study, a Swedish registry analysis described in a viewpoint whose second author co-wrote it (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), the odds ratio for schizophrenia with registry-recorded cannabis misuse fell from 10.44 in the general population to 5.07 in full siblings and to 3.52 (3.92 in the viewpoint's table) in identical twins discordant for misuse, with no significance test at the twin level and the adjustment set not stated. Three two-sample Mendelian randomization studies used genetic variants for having ever used cannabis, which explain about 1% or less of the variation in ever use where this is reported, with no adjustment beyond the source studies in the main analyses. The odds ratio for schizophrenia by genetic liability to ever use was 1.04 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.07) per doubling of the odds of ever use and 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10) by the pleiotropy-robust MR-Egger method (Gage et al., 2017); 1.08 (1.02 to 1.14) per unit of log odds, which its authors rescale to 1.37 for ever against never use (Vaucher et al., 2018); and 1.04 (p = 0.81) with five genome-wide significant variants or 1.10 (0.99 to 1.21) with 69 variants (Pasman et al., 2018). In the reverse direction, genetic liability to schizophrenia was associated with ever using cannabis (1.10, 1.05 to 1.14, per doubling, Gage et al., 2017; 1.16, 1.06 to 1.27, per unit of log odds, Pasman et al., 2018), and the genetic correlation between ever use and schizophrenia was 0.25 (Pasman et al., 2018, as corrected). These three studies share consortium data and are not independent. Narrative reviews read the evidence available to them as shared vulnerability (Ksir & Hart, 2016), as partly causal with an appreciable non-causal share (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), or as strong enough for a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk (Gage et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: Does cannabis cause psychosis? This has not been shown either way. People who use cannabis, especially often, are more likely to develop psychosis, but about half of that link shrank once other differences between people were taken into account. In a Swedish study of relatives, the link got smaller the more closely related two people were, but it was still there between identical twins, though nobody checked whether that could be chance. Gene studies found that genes linked to schizophrenia make trying cannabis more likely; evidence that genes for trying cannabis lead to schizophrenia was weaker. None of these studies looked at daily or strong cannabis. Experts reading the same studies disagree. See the contested question.
population: People in general-population cohorts, a national registry and first-episode case-control samples, and people of mostly European ancestry in genome-wide consortium data (International Cannabis Consortium, UK Biobank and 23andMe for cannabis use; Psychiatric Genomics Consortium schizophrenia cases and controls)
exposure: Cannabis use (self-reported ever or frequent use; registry-recorded misuse in the co-relative study); in Mendelian randomization, genetic liability to having ever used cannabis
comparator: People who had not used cannabis; full siblings and identical co-twins discordant for misuse; people with lower genetic liability
outcome: Psychotic disorder or schizophrenia caused by cannabis use; and, in the reverse direction, ever using cannabis predicted by genetic liability to schizophrenia
magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Attenuation of the crude association by each cohort's adjustment: about 45% on average (10% to 80%) (Moore et al., 2007). Co-relative (one registry study, misuse): OR 10.44 in the general population, 5.07 in full siblings, 3.52 or 3.92 in discordant identical twins (untested). Mendelian randomization, liability to ever use on schizophrenia: 1.04 (1.01–1.07) per doubling of the odds, MR-Egger 1.01 (0.93–1.10), 12 variants 1.03 (0.99–1.08) (Gage et al., 2017); 1.08 (1.02–1.14) per unit of log odds, rescaled 1.37 (1.09–1.67) ever vs never, 1.41 (1.09–1.83) adjusted for the variants' associations with ever smoking (Vaucher et al., 2018); 1.04 (p = 0.81) with 5 variants, 1.10 (0.99–1.21) with 69, GSMR 1.21 (p = 0.017) (Pasman et al., 2018). Liability to schizophrenia on ever use: 1.10 (1.05–1.14) per doubling (Gage et al., 2017); 1.16 (1.06–1.27) per unit (Pasman et al., 2018). Genetic correlation rg 0.25 (SE 0.03).

risk_of_bias.note: Cohort and case-control estimates remain open to residual confounding (family history, genetic liability and childhood adversity were rarely measured) and to use during an unrecognized early phase of the illness (cards sc_moore_2007, sc_di_forti_2019, sc_di_forti_2015). Mendelian randomization is observational too: the genetic design addresses confounding by environmental and social factors and, for the forward estimate, reverse causation, but its instruments are weak (0.15% to about 1% of the variance in ever use), may reach schizophrenia through other paths (risk-taking and impulsivity; only ever smoking was tested, in one study) and come from overlapping samples (cards sc_gage_2017, sc_vaucher_2018, sc_pasman_2018: ROBINS-E high for the forward estimates). The sensitivity analyses reported (MR-Egger intercepts near zero but with little power, I² 67% in one study; similar weighted-median estimates; stable leave-one-out results; no change after adjusting for ever smoking) do not justify leaving confounding unrated.

inconsistency.note: The designs point in different directions: the forward genetic estimates are positive in one study, small and method-dependent in a second and inconclusive in a third, while both studies that tested the reverse direction found it; the co-relative decline and the persistence of the cohort associations after adjustment are read in opposite ways by the critical reviews.

indirectness.note: The genetic instruments index liability to ever trying cannabis, not frequent, heavy or high-potency use, where the observational associations are largest; the co-relative study concerns registry-recorded misuse; most cohort outcomes are symptoms rather than diagnosed disorder; several figures are known only through narrative reviews.

imprecision.note: The identical-twin odds ratio was not tested for significance, and the forward genetic estimates have intervals from no effect to small effects (MR-Egger 0.93 to 1.10; 69 variants 0.99 to 1.21).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for the genetic studies; the cohort pools showed no small-study signal (Egger p = 0.48, seven cohorts).

dose_response.note: The gradient with frequency is reported in the answer on how often people use; it is not used to upgrade a causal claim because a gradient of use carries gradients of confounders and the genetic designs do not address frequency.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence, Mendelian randomization included, starts low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Counted once: the three Mendelian randomization studies share the International Cannabis Consortium exposure data (Pasman et al.'s genome-wide study includes it) and Psychiatric Genomics Consortium outcome data, so their agreement in the reverse direction is not independent replication; the co-relative figures are one registry study seen through a viewpoint by one of its authors, and the same study is read differently by Ksir & Hart (2016) and Gage et al. (2016); Hall & Degenhardt (2009) and Gage et al. (2016) restate Moore et al. (2007). A genome-wide association study shows genetic overlap, not cause; co-twin comparisons remove shared family factors, not others. Status contested: credible evidence and credible critiques point both ways, so the six-part debate box applies.

debate.question: Does using cannabis cause psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia, or do other differences between people, early illness leading to cannabis use, or shared genes explain the link?
debate.evidence_yes: In seven general-population cohorts the association remained after each cohort's own adjustment for measured confounders (about 60 across the studies, among them other substance use, personality traits, intellectual ability and other mental health problems), was larger for each cohort's most frequent use (pooled odds ratio 2.09) than for ever use (1.41), and was found for psychotic disorder (2.58) as well as for symptoms (Moore et al., 2007; see the answer on how often people use). Most of these cohorts excluded people with psychosis at the start; in the Swedish conscripts, counting only admissions at least five years after conscription gave similar results; in the Christchurch cohort, modelling suggested that cannabis predicted later symptoms rather than the reverse, and fixed-effects regression for unmeasured confounders that do not change over time made little difference (Moore et al., 2007). The review by the group that produced the potency studies adds that the Dunedin association remained after adjustment for psychotic symptoms at age 11 and that in the Christchurch cohort people tended to use less once minor psychotic symptoms appeared, which argues against self-medication (as described by Murray et al., 2016). In the one co-relative study the odds ratio was still 3.52 (3.92 in the table) in identical twins discordant for misuse, which by the viewpoint's own criteria favours a partly causal over an entirely non-causal reading (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021). Genetic liability to ever using cannabis was associated with schizophrenia in the main analysis of two Mendelian randomization studies, at 1.08 (1.02 to 1.14) per unit of log odds, stable when any single variant was left out and after adjustment for the variants' associations with ever smoking (Vaucher et al., 2018), and at 1.04 (1.01 to 1.07) per doubling (Gage et al., 2017), and by one of five methods in the third (GSMR 1.21, p = 0.017; Pasman et al., 2018). In the 11-site case-control study the odds rose from occasional to daily use and were highest for daily high-potency use (4.78 against 2.19 for daily low-potency use), and across 10 sites the incidence of psychotic disorder was higher where more controls used daily (r about 0.8) (Di Forti et al., 2019; see the answer on strong cannabis). As described in narrative reviews, high intravenous doses of THC can bring on brief psychotic symptoms in healthy volunteers (Murray et al., 2016; Gage et al., 2016; laboratory studies not read here), and two reviews judge the evidence strong enough for a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk of psychotic disorders (Gage et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2016).
debate.evidence_no: Adjustment removed on average about 45% of the crude excess odds (10% to 80% by cohort), 60% to 80% in the three most comprehensively adjusted cohorts, and no study adjusted for all major confounders: early-life adversity and shared genetic effects were rarely measured (Moore et al., 2007; Gage et al., 2016; Hall & Degenhardt, 2009). Of the cohorts reported after 2007, the association did not survive adjustment in Zurich, and in ALSPAC it fell to the null after adjustment for tobacco and other illicit drug use (1.12, 0.76 to 1.65) (Gage et al., 2016). In the one co-relative study the odds ratio fell from 10.44 in the general population to 5.07 in full siblings and 3.52 in identical twins, a 66% decline that the viewpoint reads as familial confounding accounting for more than half of the association (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021). In Mendelian randomization the evidence ran more strongly the other way: genetic liability to schizophrenia was associated with ever using cannabis (1.10, 1.05 to 1.14, per doubling, p = 2.64×10^-5, Gage et al., 2017; 1.16, 1.06 to 1.27, per unit of log odds, with similar weighted-median and GSMR estimates, Pasman et al., 2018), while the forward estimates shrank to 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10) by MR-Egger and 1.03 (0.99 to 1.08) with 12 variants (Gage et al., 2017) and were not significant with five genome-wide significant variants (1.04, p = 0.81; weighted median 0.95) or with 69 (1.10, 0.99 to 1.21) (Pasman et al., 2018). Lifetime cannabis use is genetically correlated with schizophrenia (0.25) and also with ever smoking, alcohol use, ADHD and risk-taking (Pasman et al., 2018). Specificity is doubtful: in one comparison of 9131 people with severe psychotic illness and 10,311 controls, daily tobacco smoking (odds ratio 5.11), recreational drug use (4.62) and heavy drinking (3.96) had odds ratios as large as cannabis use more than 21 times a year (3.47) (as reported by Ksir & Hart, 2016, without the adjustment set), and another review finds specificity of exposure in some studies but not all (Gage et al., 2016). The critical overview reads the family studies (most of the association disappearing after controlling for familial relationships in the Swedish registry; raised risk of schizophrenia in families of people with psychosis whether or not they used cannabis in a US family study) and the non-specificity as evidence of shared vulnerability, argues that a naturally occurring gradient of use carries a gradient of confounders, and concludes that "cannabis does not in itself cause a psychosis disorder" (Ksir & Hart, 2016). Rates of schizophrenia have not clearly followed rising cannabis use (see the answer on whether rates changed).
debate.neither_can_show: Cohort and case-control studies cannot rule out confounding by what they did not measure (family history, genetic liability, childhood adversity, premorbid functioning) or cannabis use that began during an unrecognized early phase of the illness, and adjusting for education or employment, which the illness itself may affect, can remove part of a real effect or add bias. Mendelian randomization protects against confounding by environmental and social factors that do not change genotype and, for the forward estimate, against reverse causation, but here its instruments index genetic liability to having ever tried cannabis and explain 0.15% to about 1% of its variation, so a small forward estimate says nothing about the risk with daily or high-potency use; the variants may act through traits such as impulsivity or risk-taking rather than through cannabis (only ever smoking was tested, in one study); the three studies draw on the same consortium data, with about 1500 people in both the exposure and the outcome samples of one; and the reverse estimate concerns genetic liability to schizophrenia, not diagnosed illness or its early symptoms. Weak instruments in two-sample designs bias estimates towards no effect, while overlapping samples bias them towards the observational association. A co-relative comparison removes family factors that relatives share but not those that differ between twins, and error in recording use weakens within-pair estimates more than population ones, so a decline with relatedness can overstate confounding; here it rests on one study whose twin estimate is printed two ways and was not tested. A genetic correlation above zero is expected under a causal effect as well as under confounding, so it cannot separate them on its own. Attributable fractions in these studies assume the associations are causal, and comparisons of rates across sites or over time are ecological.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). In the studies read, people who use cannabis, and especially those who use it often, are more likely to develop psychotic symptoms and disorders, and this is found in many independent cohorts. How much of that link cannabis itself causes is not known. A large part shrinks when measured differences between people are allowed for, and the one co-relative study and the genetic studies suggest that a further part reflects family background and shared genes, or genetic liability to schizophrenia making cannabis use more likely, so the evidence read here suggests the link is not wholly caused by cannabis. Whether part of it is, and how large that part is for daily or high-potency use, these designs cannot say: the identical-twin estimate stayed above 1 but was not tested, the forward genetic estimates are small, vary by method and concern only ever trying cannabis, and the case-control studies that show the largest associations with daily and high-potency use cannot rule out confounding or reverse causation. The critical reviews read here reach opposite conclusions (mostly shared vulnerability; partly causal) from overlapping evidence, and neither conclusion follows from these data alone.
debate.what_would_settle_it: Mendelian randomization with genetic instruments for frequency of use or cannabis use disorder from larger genome-wide studies, tested in schizophrenia samples that record cannabis use so that the variants' effects can be compared between people who have and have not used cannabis (a causal effect should appear only in people exposed), with multivariable adjustment for smoking, risk-taking and education; co-relative analyses in several registries reporting the numbers of discordant pairs and intervals at each level of relatedness, with use recorded before any early symptoms; prospective cohorts that record frequency and the THC and cannabidiol content of what people actually use, by product testing or biomarkers, before any psychotic symptoms, with family history and polygenic scores; and controlled before-and-after studies of the incidence of psychotic disorder where cannabis use or potency changed sharply.
